title: WHY DID JESUS RETURN TO GENESIS WHEN TEACHING MARRIAGE?
paragraphs:
WHY DID JESUS RETURN TO GENESIS WHEN TEACHING MARRIAGE?
They Asked Jesus When a Marriage Could Be Broken. Jesus Answered by Taking Them Back to Why Marriage Existed Before Anything Was Broken.
There is something almost unsettling about the way Jesus answered the question.
They came asking about divorce.
Jesus started talking about creation.
They wanted to know when a marriage could end.
Jesus took them back to the moment marriage began.
They wanted a ruling.
Jesus gave them Genesis.
And if you understand why, you may never read His words about marriage the same way again.
Because Jesus was not merely settling an argument between religious men.
He was exposing something that happens inside every human heart.
We become so accustomed to living among broken things that eventually we begin defining God's intentions by the brokenness surrounding us.
Then Jesus walks into the wreckage...
and points backward.
Back before the betrayal.
Back before the divorce papers.
Back before pornography entered the marriage.
Back before resentment made two people sleep inches apart while feeling miles away.
Back before adultery.
Back before manipulation.
Back before selfishness.
Back before somebody said, “I don't love you anymore.”
Back before humanity learned how to wound the people it once promised to protect.
Jesus went back to Genesis.
And He did it for a reason.
The confrontation begins in Matthew 19 when some Pharisees approach Jesus and test Him with a controversial question about divorce.
“Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause?”
They were asking about the boundaries.
Jesus answered by revealing the blueprint.
His response begins with words that should stop us:
“Have you not read...?”
Then Jesus reaches all the way back to Genesis.
The Greek text says:
“ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς”
ap’ archēs.
“From the beginning.”
That phrase matters.
Jesus was directing their attention beyond the debates of their generation to God's creational intention.
He says that the Creator made humanity “male and female,” echoing Genesis 1:27, and then He quotes the foundational marriage text of Genesis 2:24:
“For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”
Then comes the conclusion:
“So they are no longer two but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”
They asked Jesus about divorce.
Jesus answered with creation.
Why?
Because you cannot understand what something is permitted to become in a fallen world until you understand what God created it to be.
And Genesis tells us.
Before marriage was a government institution, it was God's design.
Before marriage had paperwork, it had covenantal reality.
Before there were wedding venues, photographers, rings, receptions, marriage licenses, lawyers, custody agreements, or divorce courts...
there was God.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was covenant union.
Genesis 1:27 records:
“זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם”
zakhar u-neqevah bara otam.
“Male and female He created them.”
Then Genesis 2:24 describes the union:
“וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ”
veda-vaq be’ishto.
“And he shall cling to his wife.”
The Hebrew verb dabaq carries the sense of clinging, sticking, holding fast.
The Greek wording quoted in Matthew likewise says that the man will be joined to his wife:
“κολληθήσεται τῇ γυναικὶ αὐτοῦ”
kollēthēsetai tē gynaiki autou.
He will be joined to his wife.
Then:
“ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν”
esontai hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Not merely two people sharing an address.
Not merely two people sharing expenses.
Not merely two people experiencing romantic attraction.
One flesh.
Marriage, in Jesus' teaching, reaches back to creation itself.
That means Jesus did not begin His theology of marriage with our feelings.
He began with God's intention.
And this is where His words become uncomfortable.
Because our culture repeatedly asks:
“What makes me happy?”
Jesus forces us to ask:
“What did God create this for?”
We ask:
“What am I allowed to do?”
Jesus asks us to remember what God has done.
We ask:
“How far can I go before technically crossing the line?”
Jesus keeps dragging our hearts back toward holiness, covenant, faithfulness, love, truth, sacrifice, and the Creator.
That principle extends far beyond marriage.
Sin constantly asks how close we can stand to the edge.
Jesus keeps calling us toward the heart of God.
But there is another detail in Matthew 19 that makes His answer even more powerful.
The Pharisees push back.
If God's design is this permanent union, why did Moses speak about divorce?
Jesus answers:
“Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.”
There it is again.
The beginning.
Jesus distinguishes between God's creational design and a concession given within a fallen world because human hearts had become hard.
And suddenly the conversation is not merely about marriage anymore.
It is about the human heart.
Hardness.
That terrifying spiritual condition where something God calls precious can eventually become disposable to us.
Where we can look into the eyes of someone made in God's image and stop seeing a soul.
Where affection becomes contempt.
Where repentance becomes defensiveness.
Where “I'm sorry” becomes impossible to say.
Where pride becomes more important than reconciliation.
Where winning the argument matters more than protecting the relationship.
Where secret messages get deleted.
Where pornography gets rationalized.
Where emotional affairs get renamed “friendship.”
Where bitterness gets rehearsed until forgiveness feels offensive.
Where two wounded people begin punishing each other for wounds neither knows how to heal.
This is why reducing Jesus' teaching to “divorce is bad” misses something enormous.
Jesus goes deeper.
He goes after the heart capable of destroying covenant.
And before anyone uses this article as ammunition against somebody else, we should allow Scripture to turn the blade toward ourselves.
Husbands cannot read Matthew 19 merely thinking about their wives.
Wives cannot read it merely thinking about their husbands.
Single people cannot dismiss it because they are not married.
Divorced people should not hear it as a declaration that grace has permanently abandoned them.
Every one of us should ask:
“Lord, where has my heart become hard?”
Because hardness of heart does not suddenly appear when divorce papers arrive.
It grows quietly.
One unresolved offense.
One hidden compromise.
One selfish habit.
One conversation continually avoided.
One apology withheld.
One secret protected.
One wound weaponized.
One temptation entertained.
One little decision after another until two people who once prayed together barely recognize each other.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You remember when you could talk for hours.
Now conversations become arguments.
You remember reaching for each other's hands.
Now you reach for your phones.
You remember praying for each other.
Now sometimes you complain about each other to everybody except God.
You remember thinking, “I cannot imagine my life without this person.”
Now perhaps you quietly wonder whether life without them would hurt less.
And maybe nobody knows.
The Facebook pictures still look beautiful.
The anniversary post was carefully written.
People commented, “Couple goals.”
You smiled at church.
You said everything was okay.
But everything is not okay.
And here is where we must handle the words of Jesus carefully.
Returning to Genesis does not mean pretending sin, betrayal, abuse, abandonment, danger, or devastating marital situations do not exist.

Scripture itself addresses grievous covenant-breaking realities, and Christians should never use “what God has joined together” as a weapon to force someone to remain physically endangered or to conceal abuse.
Biblical faithfulness does not require calling evil good.
Jesus Himself acknowledged sexual immorality in the divorce discussion of Matthew 19, and Paul later addressed abandonment by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7.
So the Christian response to a shattered marriage cannot be shallow condemnation.
Truth without compassion can become cruelty.
Compassion without truth can become permission for destruction.
Jesus gives us something better.
Grace and truth.
And that brings us to something breathtaking.
Jesus returned to Genesis because marriage does not ultimately belong to us.
God designed it.
God defines it.
And according to the wider New Testament, God gave marriage a significance even greater than companionship.
Paul quotes the same Genesis passage in Ephesians 5:
“A man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”
Then Paul says something astonishing:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Suddenly Genesis opens wider.
Marriage points beyond marriage.
The covenant between husband and wife becomes a living signpost toward the covenant love of Jesus Christ for His people.
That changes everything.
Christian marriage is not primarily two people promising to make each other perpetually happy.
It is two sinners learning to love beneath the shadow of a cross.
A husband is called to love sacrificially.
A wife is called into covenant faithfulness and respect.
Both belong first to Christ.
Both need grace.
Both need repentance.
Both need forgiveness.
Both will discover sooner or later that the person they married is a sinner.
And then comes the more disturbing discovery:
So am I.
Marriage has an extraordinary ability to expose what dating can hide.
Selfishness.
Impatience.
Pride.
Lust.
Control.
Fear.
Insecurity.
Unforgiveness.
The desire to be served rather than serve.
You may enter marriage imagining that your spouse will complete you.
Then marriage reveals that another human being cannot carry the weight of being your Savior.
Only Jesus can.
Your spouse cannot redeem you.
Your spouse cannot become your righteousness.
Your spouse cannot bear your sin before God.
Your spouse cannot fill the eternity-shaped hunger of your soul.
Christ must remain Christ.
And perhaps that is one reason some marriages collapse beneath impossible expectations.
We demand from another sinner what only a Savior can provide.
Then when they fail us, we feel betrayed by their humanity.
But the Gospel offers another way.
Two imperfect people kneeling before one perfect Savior.
Two sinners saying:
“I was wrong.”
“Please forgive me.”
“Let's pray.”
“Let's get help.”
“I don't want pride to win.”
“I don't want lust to win.”
“I don't want bitterness to raise our children.”
“I don't want our home to become another casualty of sins we were too proud to confront.”
“I want Jesus here.”
That is where Genesis meets Calvary.
Because the Bible does not end in Genesis 3.
Humanity fell.
Marriage was wounded.
Sexuality was wounded.
Families were wounded.
Trust was wounded.
Human hearts were wounded.
But God did not abandon the story.
Jesus came.
And this is where our theme becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling adultery harmless.
Not by pretending betrayal does not bleed.
Not by pretending divorce leaves no scars.
Not by pretending pornography has no victims.
Not by telling devastated spouses simply to “get over it.”
Jesus rewrites stories through redemption.
Through repentance.
Through confession.
Through truth.
Through forgiveness.
Through sanctification.
Through the cross.
Sometimes restoration means a marriage being rescued from what appeared to be its final chapter.
Sometimes it means a betrayed person discovering that Christ remains faithful even when another person was not.
Sometimes it means someone carrying the painful history of divorce finding forgiveness for their own sins and refusing to live forever under condemnation.
Sometimes it means admitting:
“I destroyed something precious.”
And then discovering that the blood of Jesus is powerful enough even for that sentence.
This must be said clearly because somebody reading this may already be divorced.
Maybe you were abandoned.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you caused enormous damage yourself.
Maybe both of you did.
Maybe you ignored every warning until there was almost nothing left.
Maybe you would give anything to travel backward.
You cannot.
Genesis is not a time machine.
But Jesus Christ is a Redeemer.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Christ's blood is sufficient.
The Gospel does not rewrite history by lying about yesterday.
Jesus rewrites the future by redeeming sinners today.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no cleansing without admitting there was dirt.
There is no repentance without admitting we were going the wrong direction.
There is no grace without acknowledging our need for grace.
So maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive words.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Jesus, my heart has become hard.”
“Jesus, I have sinned against my spouse.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding something.”
“Jesus, I need help.”
“Jesus, I don't know how to forgive.”
“Jesus, I don't know how to repair what I damaged.”
“Jesus, save me from becoming the person my bitterness is creating.”
That prayer may be more beautiful before heaven than a thousand religious performances.
And if you are married and your relationship is quietly dying, do not wait until the funeral to admit something is sick.
Bring darkness into light.
Seek wise pastoral help.
Seek appropriate professional counseling where needed.
Confess sin.
Establish boundaries.
Get serious about pornography.
Get serious about emotional affairs.
Get serious about uncontrolled anger.
Get serious about secret addictions.
Get serious about abuse and safety.
Get serious about prayer.
Get serious about Jesus.
You cannot control whether another person repents.
You cannot single-handedly manufacture reconciliation.

Forgiveness, reconciliation, trust, and restored access are related but not identical realities; rebuilding trust after serious betrayal can require truth, repentance, accountability, wisdom, and time.
But you can surrender your own heart to Christ.
And perhaps now we can finally answer the original question.
Why did Jesus return to Genesis when teaching about marriage?
Because brokenness does not get to redefine God's blueprint.
Because concessions made necessary by human sin should never make us forget God's creational intention.
Because marriage is more than romance.
Because covenant matters.
Because our bodies matter.
Because faithfulness matters.
Because holiness matters.
Because husbands and wives matter.
Because what God joins should never be treated casually.
And because marriage ultimately points beyond itself toward something greater:
Christ and His Church.
Jesus is the faithful Bridegroom.
And unlike us...
He does not break covenant.
We wander.
He remains faithful.
We hide.
He calls us into the light.
We sin.
He calls us to repentance.
We carry shame.
He carried a cross.
We deserve judgment.
He offers mercy to everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
The greatest love story in Scripture is not ultimately Adam finding Eve.
It is Christ redeeming His Bride.
Jesus did not merely teach us what covenant faithfulness looks like.
He demonstrated it with scars.
Nails through His hands.
A crown of thorns.
Blood running down His face.
A cross outside Jerusalem.
And a Savior refusing to abandon the people He came to redeem.
Then the grave opened.
And suddenly “until death do us part” was confronted by the One whom death itself could not keep.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why Christian marriage cannot be understood apart from Jesus.
Maybe your marriage needs this article.
Maybe somebody else's does.
Don't share it merely because marriage is controversial.
Send it privately to the friend whose marriage is struggling.
Send it to the engaged couple preparing for covenant, not merely a wedding.
Send it to the divorced believer who mistakenly believes their worst chapter has placed them beyond the reach of Christ.
And even send it to the person who does not yet believe, because perhaps through a conversation about marriage they will encounter the Bridegroom who gave His life for sinners.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't perform for the comments.
Be honest.

If Christ has already carried your family through something you thought would destroy it, tell your testimony. Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance, grace, counseling, perseverance, and the mercy of God can still matter.
Because there may come a night when anger feels more persuasive than covenant.
Read it again then.

And if Gospel Warrior keeps bringing Scripture into places where life actually hurts, follow us and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too. The purpose is not merely building another page. We want people opening Scripture, encountering Jesus Christ, repenting of sin, growing in truth, receiving biblical encouragement, and becoming serious disciples of Christ.
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as purchasing God's favor. You cannot buy blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or a better standing before God. Those belong to Christ and His grace.
But Christians can glorify God through cheerful, willing generosity when their support helps biblical truth reach people.
Come back to Jesus.
If your marriage is strong, bring it to Jesus.
If your marriage is wounded, bring it to Jesus.
If your marriage is hanging by a thread, bring yourself honestly to Jesus and seek wise help.
If you are single, surrender your future relationships to Jesus.
If you are divorced, bring your grief, regrets, wounds, and future to Jesus.
If you committed adultery, repent and come to Jesus.
If you were betrayed, bring the wound to Jesus.
If you have been hiding pornography, stop protecting the darkness and come into the light.
If pride has hardened you, repent.
If bitterness owns you, surrender it.
If your spouse refuses to change, remember that Christ is still Lord over your own heart.
And if your entire story looks nothing like the beautiful beginning you once imagined...
remember what Christianity has always proclaimed.
God specializes in meeting sinners after Genesis 3.
The Bible is filled with damaged people.
Broken families.
Sexual scandal.
Betrayal.
Failure.
Shame.
Tears.
Graves.
And then...
grace.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace walks directly into the darkness carrying the light of Christ.
Perhaps that is what someone needs to hear tonight:
Your broken chapter does not have more authority over your future than the crucified and risen Christ.
